title: Oscillations: understanding simple harmonic motion
voiceInstructions: Warm, engaging female teacher with a natural General American English accent. Relaxed, welcoming and lightly playful, with a gentle smile and conversational rhythm. Keep scientific terms precise and avoid an announcer cadence. Slow down for equations, numbers and conversions. Give brief natural thinking pauses after questions. Do not add words or laughter absent from the script.

sources.title: NTA: Official JEE Main 2026 syllabus, Physics Unit 10
OpenStax: Energy in simple harmonic motion

chapters.title: A restoring force, not just repetition
chapters.formula: a = -omega^2 x; T = 1/f; omega = 2 pi f
points: Measure displacement from the equilibrium position.
SHM acceleration is proportional to displacement and directed toward equilibrium.
Period is the time for one complete cycle; angular frequency is not ordinary frequency.
chapters.script: Hey, welcome back. Pull a spring gently, let go, and watch it return. Then it passes the center and comes back again. Why doesn't it simply stop at the center? The force restores it toward equilibrium, but its velocity carries it through. That balance gives us oscillation. Let's measure displacement from the equilibrium position, with right positive. For simple harmonic motion, acceleration equals minus omega squared times displacement. The minus sign is the whole story of direction: right of center, acceleration points left; left of center, it points right. Its magnitude also grows in proportion to how far we move from center. A repeating motion is not automatically simple harmonic. It must satisfy this particular acceleration rule. Period is the time for one complete cycle, returning to the same position and direction of motion. Frequency counts cycles per second. Angular frequency counts radians of phase per second and equals two pi times frequency. If an oscillator makes two cycles per second, its period is half a second and its angular frequency is four pi radians per second. Now think for a moment. At equilibrium, is acceleration largest? No, it is zero. Speed can still be largest there. Never confuse zero acceleration with zero velocity. That distinction is a favorite source of JEE mistakes.

chapters.title: Position, velocity and the meaning of phase
chapters.formula: x = A cos(omega t + phi); v = -A omega sin(omega t + phi)
points: Amplitude A is the largest displacement magnitude.
Initial phase fixes where in the cycle motion starts.
At a turning point speed is zero, but acceleration is not.
chapters.script: Picture the horizontal shadow of a point moving around a circle at constant angular speed. The shadow moves between two ends. This projection is a beautiful way to understand simple harmonic motion. We write displacement as amplitude times the cosine of omega t plus initial phase. Amplitude sets the size of the motion; omega sets how quickly it repeats; phase tells us where in that repeating cycle we are. For zero initial phase, the particle begins at the positive end, not at the center. Differentiate displacement with respect to time: velocity is minus amplitude times omega times sine of the same phase. Differentiate again and acceleration becomes minus omega squared times displacement, exactly our defining rule. Let's use amplitude four centimeters and angular frequency five radians per second. At the positive end, displacement is zero point zero four meters. Velocity is zero, while acceleration is minus one meter per second squared. A quarter period later the particle crosses equilibrium moving in the negative direction. Its velocity there is minus zero point two meters per second and its acceleration is zero. Pause and imagine those two moments. The turning point has no speed but a strong inward acceleration; the center has the greatest speed but no acceleration. For initial conditions, use both position and velocity to select phase. Position alone usually leaves two possible phases, because a particle can visit the same position while moving in opposite directions.

chapters.title: The spring sets the clock
chapters.formula: F = -kx; omega = sqrt(k/m); T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k)
points: An ideal Hooke-law spring produces SHM about equilibrium.
A heavier mass lengthens the period; a stiffer spring shortens it.
Gravity shifts a vertical spring's equilibrium, not its ideal small-oscillation period.
chapters.script: Now let's see where angular frequency comes from. An ideal spring exerts a restoring force equal to minus spring constant times displacement. Newton's second law says mass times acceleration equals this force. Divide by mass, compare with our simple harmonic motion rule, and omega squared equals spring constant divided by mass. So the period is two pi times the square root of mass divided by spring constant. This is not a formula to memorize blindly. Greater mass means more inertia and a slower response. A stiffer spring supplies more restoring force for the same displacement and gives a faster response. Take a half kilogram block on a spring of two hundred newtons per meter. Omega is twenty radians per second. The period is pi divided by ten seconds, about zero point three one four seconds. If the mass becomes four times larger with the same spring, what happens? Give yourself a moment. The square root becomes twice as large, so the period doubles, not quadruples. Within the ideal Hooke-law model, changing amplitude does not change period. Real springs can leave this model at large extensions. For a vertical spring, gravity stretches the spring to a new equilibrium. Measure displacement from that new position. The constant gravitational force cancels the equilibrium spring force, leaving the same restoring rule for the additional displacement. The period still depends on mass and spring constant, not on that equilibrium extension by itself.

chapters.title: Energy trades places through the cycle
points: For an undamped horizontal spring, total mechanical energy stays constant.
Potential energy is greatest at the ends; kinetic energy is greatest at equilibrium.
The speed formula gives magnitude; determine the velocity sign separately.
chapters.script: At the end of the motion the block stops for an instant. Where has its kinetic energy gone? Into the spring's potential energy. At equilibrium the spring's potential energy, measured from the unstretched position for our horizontal spring, is zero and kinetic energy is largest. With no friction, the total stays constant: one half spring constant times amplitude squared. At displacement x, potential energy is one half spring constant times x squared. Subtract it from total energy and you get the kinetic energy. That gives speed squared equal to omega squared times amplitude squared minus displacement squared. Notice that squaring loses the direction. Use the actual part of the cycle to decide whether velocity is positive or negative. Let's return to our half kilogram block and two hundred newtons per meter spring, now with amplitude ten centimeters. Total energy is one joule. At displacement six centimeters, spring potential energy is zero point three six joules, leaving zero point six four joules of kinetic energy. The speed is one point six meters per second. At the center it reaches two meters per second. Here's a useful JEE check: at half the amplitude, potential energy is one quarter of total energy, not one half. Kinetic energy is the remaining three quarters. Energy depends on displacement squared. With damping the amplitude and mechanical energy decrease, so the constant energy formula no longer describes the whole changing motion.

chapters.title: The pendulum and the small-angle condition
chapters.formula: theta'' = -(g/L) theta; T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g) for small angles
points: A simple pendulum model uses a point mass and light inextensible string.
The approximation sin(theta) approximately theta requires a small angle in radians.
Increasing length by four times doubles the small-angle period.
chapters.script: A swinging pendulum is another oscillator, but we must earn the simple harmonic approximation. Model the bob as a point mass on a light, inextensible string of length L. Gravity has a tangential component opposite the angular displacement. The exact tangential equation gives angular acceleration equal to minus g divided by L times sine of theta. That sine matters. For a sufficiently small angle measured in radians, sine theta is approximately theta. The equation then becomes the simple harmonic rule, with omega squared equal to g divided by L. Its period is two pi times the square root of length divided by gravitational acceleration. Bob mass cancels out. For a one meter pendulum and g equal to nine point eight meters per second squared, the period is about two point zero one seconds. If its length becomes four meters, the period becomes about four point zero one seconds, twice the original value. This assumes the same gravitational acceleration and small oscillations. A large swing takes longer than this small-angle formula predicts; don't claim amplitude independence for every pendulum swing. Let's summarize your problem-solving routine. Choose equilibrium, identify the restoring equation, check whether it is proportional to displacement, and state the assumptions. Then select a phase equation, period relation or energy equation depending on the question. Oscillations become much easier when you connect the equations to the actual motion instead of treating each one as a separate trick.

quiz.question: An oscillator has frequency 2 Hz. Its period is:
For x = 0.04 cos(5t) in SI units, acceleration at t = 0 is:
quiz.explanation: a = -omega squared x = -25 x 0.04 = -1 m/s squared.

quiz.question: A 0.5 kg mass oscillates on a 200 N/m ideal spring. Its angular frequency is:
For k = 200 N/m, m = 0.5 kg, A = 0.10 m and x = 0.06 m, speed is:
quiz.explanation: Speed = sqrt(k/m) sqrt(A squared - x squared) = 20 x 0.08 = 1.6 m/s.

quiz.question: At the same g, quadrupling pendulum length changes its small-angle period to:
quiz.explanation: Period is proportional to sqrt(L), so it doubles.
